<p class="g-kicker">The real science · vampire bat</p>
<h1>Blood, friendship, and bookkeeping.</h1>
<p class="g-lede">Everything in the game comes from real studies of real bats. Here's the
natural history behind each mechanic, and where the science is still open.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section class="g-main">
<div class="g-inner">
<div class="g-prose">

<h2>The diet</h2>
<p>The common vampire bat (<em>Desmodus rotundus</em>) feeds only on blood, mostly from
sleeping livestock, taking a few teaspoons in a 20-minute meal. The part that makes it really
tough on the bats? Blood is nearly all water and protein, so bats can't store much energy.
Gerald Wilkinson's foundational field study in Costa Rica found that adult bats come home
hungry on about <strong>7% of nights</strong> (young bats fail far more, on up to a third of
nights), and a bat that goes roughly <strong>3 nights without a meal starves to
death</strong><sup><a href="#ref-1">1</a></sup>. Every bat in a colony lives two bad nights
away from risking death.</p>

<h2>The bonds</h2>
<p>Wilkinson's 1984 <em>Nature</em> paper reported something remarkable: bats that fed
regurgitate part of their blood meal to roost-mates that didn't. The donation costs the donor
but can buy the recipient about another 12 hours of life<sup><a href="#ref-1">1</a></sup>.
Crucially, sharing wasn't limited to mothers and pups or close kin. Unrelated adults shared
too, and they shared preferentially with the individuals who had shared with them before. It
became one of the textbook cases of reciprocity in animals.</p>

<h2>The ones who invested are the ones who get rescued</h2>
<p>Thirty years later, Gerry Carter and Wilkinson tested the reciprocity claim with controlled
fasting experiments in a captive colony. They withheld food from one bat at a time and watched
who fed it. The best predictor of receiving food was not relatedness, but the amount of food
and grooming that bat had <em>previously given</em> to its potential donors
<sup><a href="#ref-2">2</a></sup>. In the game, your rescue probability is built from your
bonds (P = 0.02 + 0.60 × bond, counted over each roost-mate that fed that night). Help comes
back from the relationships you've built, and only a bat with blood can give any away.</p>

<h2>Grooming</h2>
<p>Vampire bats groom each other far more than the hygienic baseline other species
show<sup><a href="#ref-4">4</a></sup>. Grooming removes ectoparasites like bat flies and
mites<sup><a href="#ref-5">5</a></sup> (the game's mite mechanic), but it's also a social cue.
When Carter introduced strangers to each other in captivity, new relationships developed by
<strong>escalation</strong>. Bats began with low-cost grooming, "testing the water," and only
later graduated to food sharing if that bat groomed them
back<sup><a href="#ref-3">3</a></sup>. That's what the game rewards when grooming builds the
bond that later makes sharing (and rescue) likely.</p>

<h2>Nights with a bright moon</h2>
<p>Vampire bats are creatures of the dark in a strict sense. Field observations in México
found that <em>Desmodus</em> forages far less on bright moonlit nights, concentrating activity
into the darkest hours<sup><a href="#ref-6">6</a></sup>. This is a pattern called lunar
phobia, seen across many Neotropical bats, most plausibly as predator avoidance. The game's
moon cycle comes from that finding. The <em>direction</em> of the effect is sourced; the size
of the penalty on a bright night is the game's own tuning, and the storm nights that close
each season are dramatized. In reality, there is no "end" for feeding at the end of the
season, these parts just make the game more fun from a user perspective.</p>

<h2>How much to give?</h2>
<p>Donations aren't all-or-nothing. Donors regurgitate for varying durations, and the amount
transferred varies with the relationship and the donor's own condition
<sup><a href="#ref-1">1</a>,<a href="#ref-2">2</a></sup>. The sip / meal / full-crop choice in
the game reflects the bat's choice in generosity. Bigger gifts build bonds faster but cost
more of your own safety margin, so are more of a gamble!</p>

<h2>What we still don't know</h2>
<p>The open questions are the fun ones. Should a bat concentrate on a few strong bonds or
spread across many weak ones? How do reciprocity and <em>fitness interdependence</em> (having
a genuine stake in a partner's survival) interact? What happens to a relationship after a
partner defects? These are live research questions, and they're the ones
<a href="research.html">my own work</a> tackles with long-term colony data, social-network
models, and manipulative experiments. The game's dilemmas are the real dilemmas. The optimal
strategy is genuinely unsolved.</p>
